title: Unsupervised Learning: K-means, Mixtures and EM
oneLiner: Find groups in unlabelled data: K-means draws hard borders, Gaussian mixtures give soft memberships, and EM fits them.

what.html:
Unsupervised learning finds structure in data that has no labels. Clustering is the classic task: group objects so that members of a group are similar (by colour, shape, size…) and different groups are dissimilar.

Everyday versionTip a bag of mixed buttons on a table and sort them into piles without anyone telling you the categories. K-means puts each button in exactly one pile; a mixture model says "this one is 70% the blue pile, 30% the navy pile" when it's hard to tell.

This session covers K-means (hard clustering), Gaussian mixture models (soft, probabilistic clustering) and the Expectation–Maximisation (EM) algorithm that trains both.

why.html:
• Customer and user segmentation without predefined classes.
  • Compression and summarising: replace many points by a few centres (colour quantisation, vector quantisation).
  • Anomaly detection: points far from every centre, or unlikely under the mixture, are suspicious.
  • Density modelling: a mixture of Gaussians can fit multi-peaked data that a single bell curve can't.

how.title: K-means' goal: tight clusters
how.html: Pick K centres μk and assign each point to one of them so that the total squared distance from points to their centres, J = Σn Σk rnk‖xn − μk‖², is as small as possible. rnk is 1 if point n belongs to cluster k, else 0.

how.title: Two alternating steps
how.html: E-step (assign): with the centres fixed, put every point in its nearest centre's cluster. M-step (update): with the assignments fixed, move every centre to the mean of its points. Repeat until nothing changes. Each step can only lower J, so it always stops.

how.title: A worked example from the slides
how.html: Eight people (weight, glucose), K = 2, starting from candidates 1 and 2. After one round: C1 = {1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8} with centre (73.83, 182.83) and C2 = {2, 3} with centre (58, 169). The second round changes nothing, so K-means stops after 2 iterations.

how.title: Judging a clustering: SSE
how.html: The sum of squared errors (each point's squared distance to its centre) is the usual score; lower is better for the same K. But SSE always falls when K grows (K = N gives zero), so compare SSE only at equal K, or use the elbow method.

how.title: Starting points matter
how.html: K-means finds a local minimum. Unlucky initial centres can merge two real clusters and split another. Remedies: run several random starts and keep the lowest SSE, or use smarter seeding (k-means++).

how.title: Choosing K: the elbow
how.html: Plot SSE for K = 1, 2, 3, … The curve drops steeply while you're splitting real groups, then flattens. The bend ("elbow") is a sensible K. You can also just look at the data, or use domain knowledge.

how.title: Where K-means fails
how.html: K-means assumes round clusters of similar size and spread. It struggles with different sizes, different densities, non-round shapes (crescents, rings) and outliers, which drag the mean. K-medoids uses the most central actual point instead of the mean, which is far less sensitive to outliers.

how.title: Bonus: spotting outliers with K-means
how.html: For each point, divide its distance to its centre by the average distance in that cluster. A ratio well above 1 marks a likely outlier. In the glucose example, candidate 8 (weight 84) scores highest, 1.86.

how.title: Hard vs soft clustering
how.html: K-means is hard: a point near a border is forced into one cluster, and a tiny shift can flip it. A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) is soft: each point gets a probability of belonging to each cluster, so uncertainty is visible.

how.title: The bell curve and its 2-D cousins
how.html: A Gaussian is described by a mean (centre) and a spread. In 2-D the spread is a covariance matrix: equal variances give circles, unequal variances give stretched ellipses along the axes, and correlation tilts the ellipse.

how.title: A mixture of bells
how.html: Real data often has several peaks (e.g. eruption lengths of a geyser are either short or long). A GMM models the density as a weighted sum of K Gaussians: p(x) = Σ πk N(x | μk, Σk), with mixing weights πk that add up to 1. Which component produced each point is hidden ("latent").

how.title: EM: K-means with soft counts
how.html: E-step: for every point, compute its responsibility γnk, the probability that component k generated it. M-step: re-estimate each component's weight, mean and covariance using those responsibilities as soft counts. Repeat until the log-likelihood stops improving.

how.title: EM by hand on three documents
how.html: Docs (2, 2), (4, 5), (7, 2); two clusters start at means (3, 3) and (4, 4), weights 0.5. The E-step gives memberships ≈ (1, 0), (0.006, 0.994), (1, 0) and log-likelihood −12.16. The M-step moves cluster 1 to (4.49, 2.00) with weight 2.0059/3 = 0.67.

how.title: In practice
how.html: scikit-learn's GaussianMixture fits GMMs with EM (several restarts with n_init). The covariance_type option constrains shapes: "full", "tied" (shared shape), "diag" (axis-aligned) or "spherical" (round, different sizes). predict gives hard labels, predict_proba soft ones.

demo.html: Press E-step and M-step alternately and watch J fall. Then try Random restart a few times with 4 blobs and K = 4: some starts get stuck with two centres in one blob. Choose "Weight vs glucose" and K = 2 to replay the slides' example: it converges in 2 rounds.

example.html:
Grouping people by weight and blood glucose (the worked example) and clustering documents by word counts (the EM example) both come from the session.

Image intensities (slide p.29): grey levels bunch around 0, 190 and 255; a pixel halfway between 190 and 255 is better described by membership probabilities than by a hard cut.

Supplementary Network planners cluster cell sites by traffic profile (busy-hour shape, data/voice mix) with K-means to define a handful of "site types", then use a GMM's low-likelihood cells as anomaly candidates.

misunderstandings: It finds a local minimum of J that depends on the initial centres; use several restarts.
Lower SSE always means a better clustering.
SSE falls automatically as K grows; compare at equal K or use the elbow.
GMM is just K-means with circles drawn on it.
GMM gives soft memberships, different cluster shapes and sizes, and a proper probability model.
EM always finds the global maximum.
EM only climbs to a local maximum; with a component on a single point the likelihood can even blow up, so variances are floored.
takeaways: K-means minimises J = Σ r_nk‖x_n − μ_k‖² by alternating assignments (E) and mean updates (M).
Results depend on initial centres and K; use restarts and the elbow method on SSE.
K-means struggles with unequal sizes or densities, non-globular shapes and outliers; K-medoids is robust to outliers.
GMMs model data as Σ π_k N(μ_k, Σ_k) and give soft memberships.
EM: E-step computes responsibilities γ_nk; M-step updates π, μ, Σ from them; stop when the log-likelihood stabilises.
thirty: Unsupervised learning groups unlabelled data. K-means chooses K centres and assigns each point to the nearest, alternating between assigning points (E-step) and moving centres to their cluster means (M-step) until nothing changes; this lowers the within-cluster sum of squared distances. It needs a good K (elbow method), several random starts, and struggles with unequal sizes, densities, odd shapes and outliers. A Gaussian mixture model instead describes the data as a weighted sum of Gaussians and gives each point a probability of belonging to each cluster. EM fits it: compute responsibilities, then re-estimate weights, means and covariances, repeating until the log-likelihood converges.

check.q: In the K-means E-step, each point is…
opts: Given a probability for each cluster

check.q: In the M-step, each centre becomes…
opts: The mean of the points assigned to it
check.why: That minimises J for fixed assignments.

check.q: Why can't you pick K by minimising SSE alone?
opts: SSE is not defined for K > 2
SSE always decreases as K increases

check.q: Which case does K-means handle worst?
In a GMM, the responsibility γ_nk is…
opts: The probability that point n came from component k
